result: The study developed a comprehensive benchmarking framework including the synthspot simulator to generate 63 silver standards and 3 gold standards, evaluating 11 deconvolution methods (8 spatial, 1 bulk, 2 mapping) plus two baselines (NNLS and null distribution) using three complementary metrics (RMSE, AUPR, JSD). The framework is fully reproducible via a Nextflow pipeline with Docker containers.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praise the methodological rigor and reproducibility framework. Reviewer 1 states the study 'provides a reliable and reproducible evaluation framework' and notes 'a full Nextflow pipeline' and 'methods implemented in Docker containers' as strengths. Reviewer 2 highlights '(i) a full Nextflow pipeline to reproduce their analyses; (ii) methods implemented in Docker containers; (iii) a fairly decent assessment of their simulator' as elements 'above the average for a benchmarking study.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'they present a reusable and extendable platform' and notes 'the reproducibility of the methods described will have significant utility.'

result: RCTD and cell2location are the top-performing methods across silver and gold standards, with SpatialDWLS also ranking highly. Surprisingly, over half of the dedicated spatial deconvolution methods did not outperform the simple NNLS baseline, with only RCTD and cell2location consistently outperforming NNLS in challenging scenarios like dominant cell type patterns.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'The authors demonstrate the strengths of RCTD, cell2location, and SpatialDWLS for their performance, while also revealing the limitations of many methods when compared to simpler baselines.' Reviewer 2 notes 'surprisingly, several methods performed below this baseline.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'RCTD, SpatialDWLS and Cell2location typically provide the best results' and acknowledges 'many methods are still outperformed by bulk deconvolution methods (e.g. Music or NNLS).' The consistency of findings is noted as 'very similar conclusions to other deconvolution benchmarking paper' by Reviewer 3.

result: All methods showed significantly decreased performance in challenging abundance patterns, particularly with highly abundant/dominant cell types and rare cell types. RCTD and cell2location were best at detecting rare cell types, but even top-performing methods struggled when rare cell types were present in only one region. There is a strong correlation between cell type abundance and detection performance (AUPR).
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these findings without challenge. Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the results from their thorough analysis support the conclusions that creating cell type deconvolution algorithms that can handle both cell abundance and rarity throughout a given tissue sample are challenging.' The reviewers do not question the observation that performance decreases with extreme abundance patterns, and Reviewer 1 notes the study addresses 'biologically relevant, previously unconsidered aspects' including these challenging scenarios.

result: Different reference datasets can result in substantially different predicted proportions. Methods accounting for technical variability (cell2location, RCTD) showed greater stability to reference dataset changes than those that did not (e.g., SpatialDWLS). Cell2location ranked first in stability across all three tested datasets, while NNLS and MuSiC were consistently in the bottom three.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this finding, stating 'The authors make a point to address both inter- and intra- dataset reference handling, which has a significant impact on performance' and notes 'supplying optimal reference data is - potentially most - important to achieve the best performance.' Reviewer 3 also observes that 'bulk' methods like MuSiC and NNLS 'are also among the most sensitive when using an external (inter) dataset,' which aligns with the stability findings. No reviewer challenges these stability results.

result: In the liver case study with a dominant hepatocyte cell type (>60% of tissue), RCTD and cell2location were top performers achieving JSD comparable to biological variation. Methods like Tangram, DSTG, SPOTlight, and stereoscope performed worse than NNLS, with some predicting uniform distributions. The study demonstrated that using combined reference datasets did not necessarily yield best performance, and complementary metrics (AUPR and JSD) must both be considered.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the liver case study findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study includes 'case studies on liver and melanoma tissues' as part of the comprehensive evaluation. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'the authors thoroughly and rigorously compare methods while addressing situational discrepancies in model performance, indicative of a strong analysis.' The liver results are presented as validation of the silver standard findings, and no reviewer questions this validation approach or the specific performance rankings.

result: In the melanoma case study, cell2location, SPOTlight, and RCTD were the best performers with JSDs around 0.01. SPOTlight performed exceptionally well in this dataset (an exception to its silver standard performance). A qualitative analysis showed that higher-ranked methods better captured the expected trend of endothelial cells being more abundant closer to blood vessels.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the melanoma case study without challenge. Reviewer 1 mentions 'case studies on liver and melanoma tissues' as part of the evaluation scope. Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors achieve their aim to benchmark different deconvolution methods' and acknowledges the thoroughness of the analysis. The qualitative validation approach using blood vessel annotations is consistent with Reviewer 3's observation that the study demonstrates 'two approaches for evaluating deconvolution methods in datasets lacking an absolute ground truth.'

result: Most methods deconvolve silver standard datasets in less than 30 minutes with slight runtime variability. Tangram, Seurat, and SPOTlight showed constant runtime across all dimensions and processed the largest dataset in under 10 minutes. Stereoscope was the least scalable, taking over 8 hours for the largest dataset. Model-based methods (DestVI, stereoscope, cell2location, STRIDE) benefit from model reuse but require GPU acceleration.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges the importance of these findings, stating 'it's important to realize that deconvolution approaches are typically part of larger exploratory data analysis (EDA) efforts and require users to change parameters and input data multiple times. Thus, running time, computing needs, and scalability are probably key factors that researchers would like to consider when looking to deconvolve their datasets.' No reviewer challenges the runtime or scalability measurements, and the practical importance is affirmed.

result: The number of genes per cell type (correlated with sequencing depth) has a significant impact on deconvolution performance. Methods were less accurate in datasets with fewer genes per cell type (e.g., kidney dataset with <1000 genes per cell type was most challenging). The brain cortex dataset with 3000-9000 features per cell type led to much better performance despite having more cell types.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations about the impact of gene number on performance. Reviewer 3 notes 'supplying optimal reference data is - potentially most - important to achieve the best performance,' which aligns with the finding that reference quality (including gene depth) matters significantly. The observation is presented as an analysis finding without reviewer objection.

result: Results were consistent across silver standards, gold standards, and case studies (liver and melanoma), demonstrating the generalizability and applicability of the simulation and benchmarking framework.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'A key aspect of their results is that they are generally very concordant between real and synthetic datasets.' Reviewer 3 notes the study 'reach very similar conclusions to other deconvolution benchmarking paper' and that 'the authors achieve their aim to benchmark different deconvolution methods.' The consistency across different evaluation approaches is affirmed by reviewers as a strength of the study.

result: The study recommends RCTD as a good starting point due to being one of the best and fastest methods with CPU parallelization support. General guidelines include comparing multiple methods (especially cell2location and RCTD), obtaining matched scRNA-seq and spatial data from the same sample, using reference datasets with sufficient sequencing depth (>1000 genes per cell type), and using synthspot to evaluate reference quality.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these recommendations. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'provides a resource for those seeking to improve or develop new deconvolution methods,' implicitly supporting the practical guidance. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'experimental design or sample matching is at least equally important to selecting the ideal deconvolution tool,' which aligns with the recommendation to obtain matched samples. The recommendations follow logically from the benchmarking results that reviewers have accepted.

result: Existing synthetic datasets and simulators have limitations: synthetic datasets typically have random spot compositions that don't reflect tissue regions with distinct compositions; general-purpose simulators focus on other tasks and are unsuitable for deconvolution; specific simulators like scDesign3 and scMultiSim are computationally intensive and cannot model entire transcriptomes; SRTSim doesn't explicitly model tissue composition while spaSim doesn't model gene expression.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the study provides 'a fairly decent assessment of their simulator compared to other spatial omics simulators,' implicitly accepting the characterization of existing simulator limitations. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'Major strengths of the simulation engine include the ability to downsample and recapitulate several cell and tissue organization patterns,' which contrasts with the limitations of other simulators. No reviewer challenges the stated limitations of existing approaches.

result: The case studies demonstrated two approaches for evaluating deconvolution methods without absolute ground truth: (1) using proportions from another sequencing/spatial technology as a proxy, and (2) leveraging existing spot annotations (e.g., zonation, blood vessel annotations).
evaluation: Reviewers accept these methodological contributions without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the study addresses 'biologically relevant, previously unconsidered aspects.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'the authors thoroughly and rigorously compare methods' and that the study demonstrates practical evaluation approaches. The validation strategies are consistent with the reviewers' recognition of the study's thoroughness.

result: As spatial omics is an emerging field, new deconvolution methods can be anticipated. The benchmark provides a reliable and reproducible evaluation framework for current and upcoming tools, making it a valuable resource for researchers.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the study 'provides a resource for those seeking to improve or develop new deconvolution methods' and 'has the potential to also set the standard of benchmarks higher.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The Nextflow pipeline will make the prospect of including new reference datasets and new computational methods easier,' acknowledging the framework's utility for future methods. Reviewer 3 confirms 'the reproducibility of the methods described will have significant utility for researchers looking to develop cell type deconvolution algorithms.'
